p.title: Pitch Perfect: Vocal Pitch and the Emotional Intensity of Congressional Speech

ext.title: Pitch Perfect: Vocal Pitch and the Emotional Intensity of Congressional Speech
ext.venue: American Political Science Review 113(4): 941-962 (received Oct 21, 2017; accepted July 1, 2019; published online Aug 23, 2019)
ext.document_type: Journal article (empirical; includes Supplemental Information referenced but not in the text file)
ext.coverage: Read the full extracted text (2,898 lines, printed pages 941-962, including all tables, footnotes 1-33 and the reference list) in six chunks; nothing skipped. Metadata hint confirmed from the text (title, authors, APSR 113(4), pp. 941-962, DOI all match). Paul's markup: no markup files were among the input set ("(none)"), so paul_markup is empty and no highlights, underlines or sticky notes were read. Plain-text extraction drops figure images, so Figures 1-3 values come from the printed notes and prose. Table 3 group averages do not extract cleanly (Panel B pitch-difference column is garbled), so only the t-tests and text figures are relied on. The paper contains no lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation or vote-share-of-election analysis; the only election-related material is the literature review on voter responses to candidate pitch.
ext.research_question: Do small within-speaker deviations in vocal pitch (mean F0 relative to a speaker's own baseline) measure legislators' emotional intensity on an issue? Test case: do female House members speak with higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, compared with (a) male MCs on the same topic and (b) their own speech on other topics? Secondary questions: does pitch track issue commitments (women's interest-group scores; party-owned issues), and do emotionally intense female speeches about women relate to male MCs' subsequent speech and voting (p. 941-942, 944, 951)?
ext.theory: Emotional arousal tightens the vocal folds and raises pitch (Puts, Gaulin and Verdolini 2006; Owren and Bachorowski 2007; Mauss and Robinson 2009) (p. 942). Pitch is a measure of arousal/intensity, not valence (fn 1). Because pitch is hard to control, it sits low on the "leakage hierarchy" (Zuckerman and Driver 1985; Ekman et al. 1991; Kraut 1978), so it is a less strategic signal than topic choice, word choice or speech length (p. 942-944). Descriptive representation theory: female legislators have experience-based commitment to women's concerns (Reingold 1992; Mansbridge 1999), so their intensity should rise when speaking about women (p. 944-945). Signalling extension: when many women speak intensely about women, male colleagues attend and respond (Boyd, Epstein and Martin 2010; Mendelberg, Karpowitz and Oliphant 2014), with a possible backlash alternative (Kathlene 1994; Krook 2015) (p. 951, 957). Partisan extension: parties own issues and partisans speak with more intensity on owned issues (Petrocik 1996; Petrocik, Benoit and Hansen 2003) (p. 949-951).
ext.data: Source: HouseLive (Office of the Clerk) video, audio and closed-caption text for all US House floor debates, 6,432 hours from 863 debates, 2009-01-06 to 2014-08-04 (p. 944). Unit of analysis: individual floor speech of at least 50 words; N = 74,158 speeches (p. 944). Speaker sex from GovTrack; race, seniority, DW-NOMINATE and party from GovTrack/Voteview; committee chair from Stewart and Woon (2016) (p. 946). Table 1 model N: 74,151 speeches and 619 MCs (Models 1.1-1.2); 71,198 speeches and 613 MCs (Models 1.3-1.4). Female-speech counts: 13,484 speeches by women (2,403 mention women, 17.82%); 60,667 by men (5,507 mention women, 9.08%) (p. 946). Women's own speech, male-on-female-day analysis: 50,235 speeches, 509 men (Table 5). Male pitch analysis: 49,914 speeches, 506 men (Table 6). Voting analysis: 21,920 observations, 485 men (Table 7). Interest groups: 24 women's groups via Project Vote Smart, averaged per MC (p. 948). Women's bills: Volden, Wiseman and Wittmer (2018); CQ "Bills to Watch" count (p. 952). Closed captions reported ~95% accurate by the vendor; authors' transcription of 100 speeches matched (fn 11).
ext.method: Pitch: mean fundamental frequency per speech extracted with Praat (Boersma 1993 algorithm; male floor 75 Hz, ceiling 300 Hz; female range 100-500 Hz), then z-scored within speaker so units are SD above/below each MC's baseline (p. 945-946; alternative Praat windows in SI S22-S30). Topic: binary indicator for any term in Pearson and Dancey (2011b) women dictionary; alternatives are word-share and a 30-topic structural topic model (STM) (p. 945-946). Models: multilevel logit for "Women mentioned" (Models 1.1-1.2, 5.1-5.2) and multilevel linear regression for standardized pitch with random intercepts per MC (Models 1.3-1.4, 4.x, 6.x); outcome models for Table 5, 6, 7 are multilevel logit/linear with day-level Female Speeches, Female Pitch and interactions (p. 946-956). Descriptive comparisons: Welch-type t-tests across speakers and groups (Table 2; Table 3 top-25 vs bottom-25 female MCs by pitch difference; t = 2.59, df = 48). Partisan issue test: Table 4 interaction of party with party-owned STM topics. Male voting outcome: proportion of votes cast with female speakers, standardized against each male MC's prior co-voting rate (p. 955-956). Predicted values from Models 5.2, 6.1 and 7.2 at female pitch +/-2 SD (p. 953-956).
ext.identification: None causal. The paper states the design is observational and that "legislators' speeches on women simply cannot be randomly assigned" (p. 957). Within-speaker z-scoring removes stable speaker-level pitch differences (including sex differences in baseline pitch), random intercepts absorb unobserved MC heterogeneity, and a rich control set is used (race, seniority, chair, DW-NOMINATE, party, one-minute speech, duration, election year). Placebo tests and dyadic models are in SI S55-S62. Male-response models restrict to men who spoke on the same legislative day as women's speeches and add agenda controls (Women's bills, CQ bills). The volume-times-pitch interaction is the key test. Robustness: results unchanged under alternative DV operationalizations (word share, STM) (p. 946), re-estimated without observations beyond +/-2 SD (fn 28, p. 953), and different Praat pitch windows (p. 945-946).
ext.scope: Population: all US House floor speeches of at least 50 words during the 111th-113th Congresses (Jan 2009 to Aug 2014), roughly 77-81 women in the House in that span (p. 956). Institution: US House floor only (not the Senate, committees, or state legislatures, which the authors name as future audio sources, p. 958). Era: 2009-2014. Speeches are natural floor speech, not acted or induced emotion (p. 944). The authors explicitly do not claim general causal effects of women's speech on male behavior (p. 957).
measures: Standardized mean F0 (vocal pitch) per speech, in SD above/below speaker baseline (Praat; Titze 2000 F0 framework)
Raw mean F0 in Hz (Table 2 and footnote 15)
Women-mention dictionary indicator (Pearson and Dancey 2011b), with word-share and STM alternatives
Party, DW-NOMINATE, seniority, committee chair, race, one-minute speech, speech duration, election year
Pitch difference: mean Hz when mentioning women minus not mentioning (Table 3)
Women's interest-group scores: average of 24 Project Vote Smart scorecards
Women's bills introduced (Volden, Wiseman and Wittmer 2018) and CQ Bills to Watch (count per legislative day)
Party-owned issue topics from a 30-topic STM (9 Democratic-owned, 9 Republican-owned categories)
Female Speeches (count per day of women's speeches mentioning women) and Female Pitch (their average standardized pitch)
Male co-voting with female speakers, standardized against each male MC's prior co-voting (Voteview votes)

key_findings.finding: Women are more likely than men to reference women in floor speeches.
key_findings.numbers: 17.82% of female speeches (2,403/13,484) vs 9.08% of male speeches (5,507/60,667); predicted probability 0.17 vs 0.08 (2.13 times). Holds with controls (Model 1.2).

key_findings.finding: Female MCs speak at higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, and male MCs do not.
key_findings.numbers: Female x 'Women mentioned' = 0.090 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) without controls and 0.112 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) with controls. Female MCs: +0.09 SD when referencing women, about five times the male change of +0.02 SD. Male pitch unchanged (t = 0.02, df 58,281). Democratic women t = 3.12; Republican women t = 2.81.

key_findings.finding: Raw pitch levels: female MCs' pitch rises on speeches mentioning women; male pitch is flat.
key_findings.numbers: Female MCs: 206.01 Hz when mentioning women vs 203.27 Hz otherwise. Male MCs: 151.50 Hz vs 151.49 Hz. Republican women 207.02 Hz vs Democratic women 205.68 Hz when mentioning women (not significantly different, fn 15).

key_findings.finding: Among female MCs, the most emotionally intense on women's issues have higher women's interest-group scores.
key_findings.numbers: Top 25 vs bottom 25 female MCs by pitch difference: difference in Vote Smart scores t = 2.59, df = 48, p < 0.02. Democratic women only: t = 2.83, df = 39, p <= 0.01. Republican women: t = 0.14, df = 7, not significant (small N). Table 3 group averages are not reliably extracted and are not relied on.

key_findings.finding: Partisans speak with higher pitch on their party-owned issues and lower pitch on the opposing party's issues.
key_findings.numbers: Democrat x Democratic-owned issues = 0.328 (Model 4.1) and 0.288 (Model 4.2), both p<0.01. Republican x Republican-owned issues = 0.380 (Model 4.3) and 0.355 (Model 4.4), both p<0.01. Democrats use 9.02% more words on Democratic-owned topics; Republicans use 17.21% more on Republican-owned topics (t = 18.43 and 30.51). Topic shares capture under 8% of words per speech on average.

key_findings.finding: Male MCs mention women more often on days with more female speeches on women, and more so when female pitch is high in the interaction model.
key_findings.numbers: Table 5 Model 5.2: Female speeches = 0.060 (SE 0.003); Female speeches x Female pitch = 0.011 (p<0.05). Figure 1 (Female pitch +2 SD): going from 0 to 43 female speeches raises P(male mention of women) from 0.05 to 0.56. From 6 to 11 speeches (1 SD either side of mean): 0.07 to 0.10. Model 5.1 interaction is not significant at 0.05.

key_findings.finding: Male MCs' pitch on women rises with the volume and intensity of female speeches on women.
key_findings.numbers: Three-way interaction (Women mentioned x Female speeches x Female pitch) = 0.016 (SE 0.005, p<0.01). At Female pitch +2 SD, raising female speeches from 6 to 11 moves male pitch on women from 0.17 SD to 0.26 SD; from 0 to 43 moves it from 0.12 SD to 1.79 SD.

key_findings.finding: Male co-voting with female speakers rises with the volume and intensity of women's speeches; no backlash detected.
key_findings.numbers: Female speeches x Female pitch = 0.015 (Model 7.1, p<0.01) and 0.012 (Model 7.2, SE 0.002, p<0.01). At Female pitch +2 SD, the standardized co-voting rate rises from -0.23 SD to +0.53 SD as female speeches go from 0 to 43 (p. 956). Authors read this as no evidence of male backlash (p. 957).

key_findings.finding: The maximum observed volume of female speeches on women is large relative to the chamber.
key_findings.numbers: 43 female speeches on women on one day = 56% of the 77-81 women in the 111th-113th Congresses.

key_findings.finding: Results are robust to alternative outcome measures and to trimming extreme pitch values.
key_findings.location: p. 946 (alternative DVs); fn 28, p. 953 (+/-2 SD trim); SI S30-S36, S66-S69
key_findings.numbers: Word-share and STM operationalizations of women-topic give identical substantive results. Trimming pitch beyond +/-2 SD is 'generally robust' (no numbers reported in text).

limitations: Observational design; the authors say they do not claim causal effects of female MCs' intense speech on male behavior, and that alternative explanations cannot be ruled out (p. 957).
Male response is not zero at low female participation: at few female speeches the effect is absent or negative, so the signalling story is conditional on volume (p. 957).
Backlash is examined only with one voting measure and cannot be ruled out in other outcomes; votes may come before or after speeches because the data have no time stamps (fn 31, p. 955-956).
Pitch-based intensity is an arousal measure, not valence; a single pitch number cannot say whether a speaker is enthusiastic or angry (fn 1, p. 942).
Mean F0 per speech is a coarse measure; other factors (question intonation, duration) also move mean pitch, though controls are included (fn 8, p. 945; p. 958-959).
Women-topic is a coarse dictionary indicator; alternatives used as robustness checks (p. 945-946).
Effect size is small: 0.09 SD for female MCs on women's topics, which the authors concede is 'slight' and likely below conscious control (p. 947).
Confidence and expertise could explain some intensity; the paper does not separate them, and male MCs with the most women's bills did not show the same pattern (fn 19, p. 948).

Republican-owned and Republican-women effects are weaker or not significant in some specifications, partly due to small N of Republican women (p. 948-949; fn 17; t = 0.14 with df = 7 for Republican women in Table 3 comparison).
Male MCs' floor attendance is unobserved; the sample uses all male MCs who spoke the same day as a proxy for exposure (fn 24, p. 953).
Closed-caption text is ~95% accurate per the vendor (fn 11, p. 945).
Table 3 group averages do not extract cleanly from the PDF text; only the reported t-tests are used here.
Single chamber (US House) and single era (2009-2014); generalization to other chambers or periods is untested (p. 958-959).

rel.summary_md:
Dietrich, Hayes and O'Brien use 74,158 US House floor speeches from 2009 to 2014, each at least 50 words, taken from Clerk HouseLive audio. They measure each speech's mean vocal pitch (F0, extracted with Praat) and z-score it against the speaker's own baseline. They argue this is a hard-to-fake measure of arousal. It tracks intensity, not valence (footnote 1). Female members speak about 0.09 to 0.11 SD above their baseline when they mention women, while male members do not change (Table 1). Partisans speak about 0.29 to 0.38 SD higher on topics their party owns (Table 4). On days when many women speak with high pitch about women, male members mention women more, raise their own pitch on the topic, and co-vote more with the women speakers (Tables 5-7). These response results are observational, and the authors say they are not causal (p. 957).

The system has already built this method. `fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:209-254` cites the paper by name and computes `pitch_deviation_from_speaker_baseline_z` and `topic_emotional_intensity`. The two differ in three ways. The paper relies on a cross-speaker contrast (female versus male, times topic) and roughly 120 speeches per speaker. The system reports a per-speaker topic mean with no comparison group. Its floors are 5 speech units per member, 2 topics, and 2 units per topic (`fec/audio_rules.py:20-22`). Effects of 0.1 to 0.4 SD cannot be detected at those floors. With only two topics, the sign of each topic's deviation is fixed by construction. The paper also measures in one floor venue with one channel. The system's baseline is pooled across interview programs and channels. The paper supports the system's existing rules: absolute F0 stays out of personality scores, and audio stays display-only. It also points to a better identity source: Clerk floor video, where the chamber has already identified the speaker.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotional intensity is measured as each speech's mean F0 z-scored against the speaker's own baseline, in SD units. Detecting the effect needed about 120 speeches per member on average (74,151 speeches from 619 members). The female × women-mentioned effect is 0.090 SD (SE 0.027) without controls and 0.112 SD with controls. The party-owned-issue effect is 0.29-0.38 SD. The authors call the 0.09 SD effect 'slight'.
bearings.system_side: The candidate v2 descriptor converts eGeMAPS semitones to Hz and cites Dietrich, Hayes & O'Brien in a code comment. It z-scores each speech unit against the member's mean and SD and reports `topic_emotional_intensity` as the mean deviation per topic. Required floors: at least 5 speech units per member, at least 2 topics, and at least 2 units per reported topic. No comparison group is used. The output is a candidate artifact that nothing consumes (status CANDIDATE_CONSUMED_BY_NOTHING_AWAITING_USER_RATIFICATION), and the v2 artifact holds 0 accepted clips.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transform (within-speaker z of mean F0) carries over directly. The inference does not. Dietrich's evidence is a difference-in-differences across speakers over thousands of speeches. A single member's topic mean from 2-5 units has an SE of roughly 0.45-0.7 SD, larger than every effect the paper reports. With exactly 2 topics, the two topic deviations must have opposite signs by construction (their unit-weighted sum is zero). The paper used floor speech from one Clerk source. The system uses on-air interviews across outlets and channels, which the paper never tested.

bearings.paper_claim: Mean F0 also moves with question intonation, speech duration and speech type (one-minute speeches), so the paper adds these as controls. The baseline comes from one venue (House floor, HouseLive). Pitch measures arousal, not valence.
bearings.system_side: The baseline is pooled across all accepted units from at least 2 programs and 2 sources. Channel (studio, remote or telephone) is recorded in the brain as uncontrolled. Neither the per-member z nor the WJ subject_effects centering controls for duration or questions. The Washington Journal subject_effects shown on the desk report per-member topic pitch shifts from as few as 2 reactions.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies wherever the system compares a member's pitch across topics. Channel and venue differences shift F0 by more than the paper's 0.1 SD effects, so a topic that appears mostly on one program will pick up that program's offset. The 'meaning' string calls the output 'relative emotional intensity', which is safe only as arousal. It must never be read as anger or enthusiasm.

bearings.paper_claim: Raw F0 differs mostly by sex (female 203-206 Hz vs male about 151 Hz, Table 2). The intensity signal is the deviation from each speaker's own baseline, so stable between-speaker pitch differences carry no intensity information. The measure is a topic-level state, not a trait.
bearings.system_side: The output contract sets 'absolute_f0_enters_personality': False and 'audio_may_modify_big_five': False. It explicitly excludes 'absolute F0 or inferred gender as a personality input'. The brain records that pitch_variability_raw is sex-confounded (r = -0.266) and that the audio-prosody N pilot MISSed at N = 90.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The support is direct. The paper's design removes between-speaker level by construction, so it offers no evidence that pitch measures a between-member disposition such as N. This agrees with the closed audio-N route and the display-only ruling.

bearings.paper_claim: The corpus is the Office of the Clerk's HouseLive video, audio and closed captions, 6,432 hours across 863 debates, where the chamber has already attributed each speech to a member. The vendor reports captions as about 95% accurate, and the authors' check of 100 speeches matched.
bearings.system_side: Clips are kept when Haiku 4.5 reads them from YouTube auto-captions as SOLO_TARGET and MATCH or NEUTRAL. The brain records that about 33.7% of kept clips rest on evidence with no identifying content. Search-fetched floor audio had about 38% contamination before the 2026-07-09 fix.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This applies only to House floor audio, and only from 2009 onward, where Clerk video carries speaker identification. It would not cover interviews, Sunday shows, Senate audio or hearings. It would replace the guessed identity on floor clips with the chamber's own record, but it does not touch the interview corpus where the identity gap is largest.

bearings.paper_claim: Text features such as topic choice, word choice and length sit high on the leakage hierarchy, so speakers control them strategically. Vocal pitch largely lies beyond the speaker's control. The paper offers audio as a measure of intensity that text cannot give.
bearings.system_side: Press intensity is |LSD net| / words or (pos+neg)/words on member press releases. The press pillar multiplies stance sign by this 'heat'. The brain note treats it as how heated a release is.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a theoretical argument, not a test of LSD. The paper never compares dictionary tone with pitch. Press releases are drafted by staff, so they are even more strategic than floor speech. LSD intensity therefore measures crafted rhetorical tone, not felt intensity, and should be labelled that way. It does not invalidate the tone term as a measure of messaging emphasis.

bearings.paper_claim: Male MCs' same-day co-voting with female speakers rises with Female speeches × Female pitch: 0.015 (Model 7.1) and 0.012 (Model 7.2, SE 0.002). At +2 SD pitch the standardized co-voting rate moves from -0.23 to +0.53 SD as speeches go from 0 to 43. The male response is absent or negative at low volume.
bearings.system_side: Linear-threshold priming sums neighbour pressure against a tier threshold. The cue weight depends only on bipartisanship (sqrt(bpf_u bpf_v)), with no term for the intensity of the signal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The result is observational and gender-specific (women's issues, 2009-2014). It concerns floor co-voting within a day, which has no time stamps, so votes may come before the speeches. It is not about cosponsorship. The pattern of no response at low volume and a response at high volume is compatible with threshold adoption, but it does not test it. It should not be used to set any engine constant.

gaps_exposed: No comparison group. The paper's evidence is a cross-speaker contrast (female vs male, times topic), but topic_emotional_intensity reports one member's topic mean with nothing to compare it against (b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:237-249).

Power. The floors are 5 units per member, 2 topics and 2 units per topic (audio_rules.py:20-22). At those floors the SE of a topic mean is roughly 0.45-0.7 SD, while the paper's effects are 0.09-0.38 SD and needed about 120 speeches per member. No minimum detectable effect is reported anywhere.

The sign is fixed by construction when a member has 2 topics. The brain records a within-member permutation-null fix (sign_informative, commit 4193f0140 on the unmerged speech-recognition branch), but the live b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py has no null or sign_informative field. UNVERIFIED drift between brain and live tree.

No controls for question intonation, speech duration or speech type, and no venue or channel term, in either the per-member z or the WJ subject_effects (build_descriptive_speech.py:2491-2531). The paper treats these as confounds of mean F0.
The floor-speech audio does not use Clerk HouseLive, where the chamber has already attributed each speech to a member. The system instead verifies identity from captions with an LLM.
No issue-ownership check. The paper's party-owned-topic pitch effect (0.29-0.38 SD) gives a ready external sanity check for any topic-pitch descriptor, and the system has not run it.
flags: The desk shows per-member topic pitch shifts from as few as 2 WJ reactions (build_descriptive_speech.py:2521; make_member_desk_00.tpl:1280). The window and count are shown, but at that n the values are noise relative to the paper's effect sizes. Treat them as UNVERIFIED descriptive output, never as an intensity finding.

The brain says topic_emotional_intensity was fixed with a permutation null, but the live candidate file lacks it. This is a committed-vs-live discrepancy, and per DE-062 it stays UNVERIFIED until a second check of the branch.

The paper's male-response results (Tables 5-7) are observational and gender-specific (authors, p. 957). Any import into cascade or threshold constants would be unvalidated. Do not describe them as influence probabilities.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025. The paper does not touch cosponsorship edges, edge normalization or LDA.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul lists this paper as on disk without annotation, under his interest in non-textual channels for the prosody component. The paper confirms that pitch can carry a real signal, but only as a within-speaker state (arousal by topic), only with large samples, and only through cross-speaker contrasts. That matches the system's ruling that audio is display-only and never feeds the Big Five scores (b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:358). His note is out of date in one way: the method has already been transplanted, and the code cites the paper by name at b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:210. The open question is no longer whether to use pitch. It is whether the implementation meets the paper's sample and comparison requirements, and at current floors it does not. His margin note on Joo ('Monitoring tool?') concerns a different Dietrich paper, on video and aisle crossing, not this one.

related.why: Covers the general pitfalls of audio as political data (alignment, feature choice, classifiers) that this paper's single-venue pitch design sidesteps. Together they inform whether the system's cross-venue interview baseline is defensible.

Both measure elites from speech. Ramey reads traits from words, while Dietrich argues words are strategic and pitch less so. This is the text-versus-voice tension behind the lexical Big Five and audio lanes.
The brain uses Salam to sex-condition prosody features. Dietrich's within-speaker z is the alternative fix for the same sex confound in F0.

Marrero asks whether voice carries trait (personality) information. Dietrich's design deliberately strips between-speaker level and treats pitch as a topic-level state, which argues against reading traits from F0.
Joo's piece on non-text political data is where Paul's margin note about Dietrich's video work sits. This paper is the audio counterpart in that line of work.
